q: For which regimes (t/N, P) is the paper's 8/pi^2 success-probability floor actually tight? Our 90-config sweep gave exact success probabilities ≥ 0.99 in every case, well above the theoretical 0.811. Where does the theorem's guarantee bite in practice?
basis: Direct observation from our exact-QPE marginal computation: computing the total probability that the measurement lands in the theorem's success set gave values ≫ 8/pi^2 across all N ∈ {16,32,64} and t sweeps. The paper proves a lower bound but does not characterize its tightness.
next_steps: Extend the analytic-QPE sweep to a fine grid in (t/N ∈ [0,1], p) with a much denser resolution near t/N ∈ {0, 1/2, 1}; compute the exact success probability and locate the argmin. Compare to a numerical construction of adversarial (t, N, P) triples that saturate the Dirichlet-kernel worst case.

q: What is the actual worst-case absolute error of the argmax decoding rule (as opposed to the paper's existential bound)? Our sweep saw argmax errors ≤ 5.25 (n=6, t=25, p=4) but no systematic worst-case scan.
basis: We only sampled random marked-index sets and a few t values per n. The paper bounds ANY output of the counting algorithm but does not specifically address argmax decoding; empirically argmax was always within-bound but the tightness across all (t,N,p) is unknown from our data.
next_steps: Enumerate all t ∈ {0,1,...,N} for N ≤ 128 and compute argmax-error over all (p ∈ {2,...,10}); build a surface max_error(t/N, log P/log N) and identify the worst regions. Cross-check against Corollary 2's implied worst-case.

q: How do modern decoding rules (median-of-two-peaks, matched filter on the Dirichlet kernel, iterative refinement) compare to the paper's original bound? The paper output is essentially argmax; but the two-peak symmetry suggests a symmetric decoder could halve the variance.
basis: The exact marginal in our simulator is a two-lobed function symmetric around f = P/2, with equal weight at phi_+ and phi_-. A decoder using both peaks (their weighted average, or maximum likelihood over the two lobes) could reduce single-realisation error but was not explored.
next_steps: Implement median, weighted-average, and matched-filter decoders on the same 90-configuration sweep and report empirical error distributions. Prove or disprove a tighter probability bound for the two-peak MAP decoder.

q: How does the Theorem-5 bound degrade under realistic noise (depolarising / dephasing on the counting register and the Grover iteration)? The paper analysis is unitary; on real hardware the phase-kickback fidelity drops per controlled-G^{2^k} step.
basis: Our replication is fully coherent (Qiskit Statevector), so it cannot address noise effects. But the counting circuit uses O(P) applications of G, so a per-gate error rate ε accumulates as ~ P·ε per counting-qubit slot; the paper's success guarantee should degrade as this crosses O(1).
next_steps: Repeat a subset of the sweep on the qiskit-aer 'density_matrix' backend with a parameterised depolarising channel per gate; measure the fitted breakdown ε_crit(N, P). Compare to the analytical error-propagation prediction for QPE under noise (e.g., Cleve et al.).

q: At fixed query budget, does iterative amplitude estimation (Grinko et al. 2019) or Bayesian phase-estimation (Wiebe & Granade) outperform vanilla counting on the same (t, N) grid, and by how much?
basis: The paper's counting is one point on the accuracy-vs-queries curve. Modern iterative variants claim comparable Θ(1/ε) query complexity with far fewer counting qubits (so far easier on NISQ hardware). Our replication has an exact QPE simulator that could serve as a baseline.
next_steps: Implement iterative amplitude estimation (Grinko 2019) and canonical Bayesian phase estimation using the same G operator; run identical (N, t) grids and compare (i) total controlled-G calls, (ii) achieved |t - t̂|, (iii) counting-qubit count. Report the crossover regime where each method dominates.
